newsitem.title: UK: Clarke defends British government over EMU.
newsitem.headline: Clarke defends British government over EMU.

text.p: Finance minister Kenneth Clarke on Monday took the sting out of a furious row in Britain's ruling Conservative Party by assuring parliament London would not be bound by rules for the European Union's planned single currency.

Prime Minister John Major negotiated an opt-out from economic and monetary union (EMU) in 1991, but Conservative "Eurosceptics" had voiced concern and anger at what they saw as an attempt by the government to smother debate over the rules.

Clarke, forced to take time off from preparations for Tuesday's make-or-break budget, told restless members of parliament that there was no question of Britain's hands being tied as long as it remained outside the single currency.
"Any recommendations that might be made... are non-binding," Clarke said in an emergency statement to the House of Commons.
The statement was crucial because Conservative strategists agree that the party's cracks over Europe need to be papered over for it to have any chance of winning the next election.
The Labour Party, in opposition since 1979, enjoys a 20 percentage point lead in opinion polls, with a general election due by May 22 at the latest.
Clarke said some press reports about the proposed single currency rules had been "highly misleading".

Eurosceptics fiercely opposed to closer European integration had feared that Clarke, at a meeting of EU finance ministers in Brussels next week, would endorse rules for EMU before parliament had been given a chance to scrutinise them.

But Clarke said no EMU legislation was likely to come up for formal adoption next week, giving parliament a chance to debate the issues fully before the December 12/13 EU summit in Dublin -- the earliest occasion for binding decisions to be taken.

The finance minister, whose budget could hold the key to the Conservatives' electoral fortunes, said he was releasing some hitherto confidential documents to show he was serious about welcoming the opportunity for a full and informed debate.
"Whether we are in or out (of EMU), my concern is and will remain to respect the position and traditions of this parliament and our independent nation state," Clarke told MPs.
In a separate step aimed at placating his rank and file, aides said Major had agreed to hold an extended parliamentary debate on the EU before the Dublin summit.
He also held what one official called a constructive meeting with a deputation of Conservative MPs dispatched to complain about the government's handling of the EMU issue.

The initial reaction suggested that Clarke had managed to soothe the Conservatives' worst fears that Britain -- despite its opt-out -- was somehow taking a further irreversible step toward EMU, due to start in 1999.

Clarke's predecessor as chancellor of the exchequer, Norman Lamont, agreed that plans for a German-sponsored "stability pact" imposing fines on EMU members with big budget deficits would not bind Britain.

But another leading Eurosceptic, John Redwood, urged Clarke to insist on a written promise that Britain would be exempt from the proposed constraints unless it joined EMU. "There are different legal views about the current loose wording," he said.

A third Eurosceptic former minister, David Heathcoat-Amory, told Clarke: "This unnecessary row could have been resolved much earlier by the granting of a full debate about an issue which the prime minister said himself is the most important decision facing the country."
